The board should not treat “uranium supply risk” as one risk: mining, transport, conversion, enrichment, fuel fabrication, and reactor-specific qualification are separate links, and a failure at any one of them can delay fuel even when uranium ore is plentiful. The reassuring part is that uranium is not economically analogous to gas: fuel is a relatively small component of nuclear generation cost, so even a doubling of the uranium price from $25 to $50 per pound in one historical analysis increased generation cost by about 10%, whereas fuel can represent roughly 90% of the marginal cost of gas generation. That does not make fuel disruption harmless, because a reactor needs qualified, correctly fabricated fuel on schedule, not merely an affordable quantity of yellowcake. Mining risk is concentrated geographically, with Kazakhstan historically the largest producer and an example of how political unrest there caused uranium prices to jump sharply. Kazakhstan’s importance is not only geological: substantial exports have used routes through Russia, so sanctions, border restrictions, shipping interruptions, or payment problems can disrupt supply even when the mine itself continues operating. Mining is therefore a medium-term price and availability risk, not normally an overnight “the plant has no fuel tomorrow” risk, because utilities, governments, traders, and the fuel cycle hold inventories and because secondary sources such as re-enrichment and recycled material can provide some cushion. The more acute structural concern is often mid-cycle capacity: only a small number of facilities worldwide perform conversion, enrichment, and specialized fabrication, and those services are technically demanding and tied to particular reactor designs. Conversion turns milled uranium into uranium hexafluoride suitable for enrichment, enrichment raises the U-235 concentration, and reconversion and fabrication turn the enriched material into pellets, rods, and assemblies that fit a specified reactor. Russia matters disproportionately at these mid-cycle steps: one assessment puts Russia at approximately one-third of global conversion supply and about 43% of global enrichment capacity, while the United States has historically obtained a substantial share of its enriched fuel through Russian-linked supply. This means replacing Russian supply is not principally a question of opening more mines, because new mines cannot immediately substitute for missing conversion or enrichment capacity. A Russian cutoff would more plausibly create a procurement squeeze, longer lead times, higher conversion and enrichment prices, and competition for non-Russian capacity than an immediate worldwide uranium shortage. Historical analysis estimated that Western reactors could begin feeling a Russian converted-or-enriched-fuel interruption within roughly 18 to 24 months because fuel orders require substantial advance notice, although the precise timing depends on inventories, reactor requirements, and available substitute capacity. Recent price spikes should therefore be read as signals of tightness and investment stress, not as a direct forecast of electricity prices: spot uranium represents only a small portion of total consumption, while long-term contracts and service contracts dominate actual utility procurement. The price risk is nevertheless real because low prices discourage mine development and new conversion or enrichment capacity, whereas higher forward prices are needed to finance projects that may take years to build and qualify. Long-term contracting helps by reserving material and capacity, supporting new-project financing, reducing exposure to spot-market spikes, and giving the utility time to plan around delivery schedules. It does not provide absolute protection unless the contract covers the whole required chain, because a contract for uranium concentrate does not by itself guarantee conversion slots, enrichment work, fabrication capacity, transport, or an alternative qualified fuel design. A utility should ask whether its proposed agreement is a fixed-price, indexed-price, or market-linked arrangement, whether it contains volume and delivery guarantees, and whether the supplier can demonstrate contracted access to conversion, enrichment, fabrication, transport, and backup inventory rather than only to uranium in the ground. The agreement should also specify force-majeure treatment, sanctions and geopolitical substitution rights, notice periods, supplier-default remedies, replacement-fuel costs, minimum inventory, and who pays if a supplier must move material through a more expensive route. The board should require diversification by supplier, country, route, and fuel-cycle stage rather than accepting a superficially diversified list of mines that all depend on the same Russian conversion or enrichment pathway. It should also require the project company to report annually on forward coverage, on-site and off-site inventory, qualified alternative fabricators, non-Russian enrichment access, and the time required to qualify a substitute fuel. An ordinary light-water SMR generally has the familiar low-enriched-uranium problem, with conventional fuel enriched to roughly 3% to 5% U-235, so its supply challenge is mainly access to diversified LEU, conversion, enrichment, and fabrication. The board should not treat “uranium supply risk” as one risk: mining, transport, conversion, enrichment, fuel fabrication, and reactor-specific qualification are separate links, and a failure at any one of them can delay fuel even when uranium ore is plentiful. [shard_04764_4126] [shard_02602_34449]

The reassuring part is that uranium is not economically analogous to gas: fuel is a relatively small component of nuclear generation cost, so even a doubling of the uranium price from $25 to $50 per pound in one historical analysis increased generation cost by about 10%, whereas fuel can represent roughly 90% of the marginal cost of gas generation. [shard_04516_9176]

That does not make fuel disruption harmless, because a reactor needs qualified, correctly fabricated fuel on schedule, not merely an affordable quantity of yellowcake. [shard_04764_4126] [shard_04912_28668]

Mining risk is concentrated geographically, with Kazakhstan historically the largest producer and an example of how political unrest there caused uranium prices to jump sharply. [shard_00440_62819] [shard_04155_17350]

Kazakhstan’s importance is not only geological: substantial exports have used routes through Russia, so sanctions, border restrictions, shipping interruptions, or payment problems can disrupt supply even when the mine itself continues operating. [shard_05762_6555] [shard_04912_28668]

Mining is therefore a medium-term price and availability risk, not normally an overnight “the plant has no fuel tomorrow” risk, because utilities, governments, traders, and the fuel cycle hold inventories and because secondary sources such as re-enrichment and recycled material can provide some cushion. [shard_05480_7160] [shard_02824_2185]

The more acute structural concern is often mid-cycle capacity: only a small number of facilities worldwide perform conversion, enrichment, and specialized fabrication, and those services are technically demanding and tied to particular reactor designs. [shard_04912_28668] [shard_04764_4126]

Conversion turns milled uranium into uranium hexafluoride suitable for enrichment, enrichment raises the U-235 concentration, and reconversion and fabrication turn the enriched material into pellets, rods, and assemblies that fit a specified reactor. [shard_04764_4126]

Russia matters disproportionately at these mid-cycle steps: one assessment puts Russia at approximately one-third of global conversion supply and about 43% of global enrichment capacity, while the United States has historically obtained a substantial share of its enriched fuel through Russian-linked supply. [shard_04912_28668] [shard_02768_44044]

This means replacing Russian supply is not principally a question of opening more mines, because new mines cannot immediately substitute for missing conversion or enrichment capacity. [shard_04912_28668] [shard_01427_71709]

A Russian cutoff would more plausibly create a procurement squeeze, longer lead times, higher conversion and enrichment prices, and competition for non-Russian capacity than an immediate worldwide uranium shortage. [shard_01427_71709] [shard_01504_57750]

Historical analysis estimated that Western reactors could begin feeling a Russian converted-or-enriched-fuel interruption within roughly 18 to 24 months because fuel orders require substantial advance notice, although the precise timing depends on inventories, reactor requirements, and available substitute capacity. [shard_01427_71709]

Recent price spikes should therefore be read as signals of tightness and investment stress, not as a direct forecast of electricity prices: spot uranium represents only a small portion of total consumption, while long-term contracts and service contracts dominate actual utility procurement. [shard_01504_57750] [shard_03095_68102]

The price risk is nevertheless real because low prices discourage mine development and new conversion or enrichment capacity, whereas higher forward prices are needed to finance projects that may take years to build and qualify. [shard_00440_62819] [shard_01868_5915] [shard_01504_57750]

Long-term contracting helps by reserving material and capacity, supporting new-project financing, reducing exposure to spot-market spikes, and giving the utility time to plan around delivery schedules. [shard_03095_68102] [shard_01868_5915]

It does not provide absolute protection unless the contract covers the whole required chain, because a contract for uranium concentrate does not by itself guarantee conversion slots, enrichment work, fabrication capacity, transport, or an alternative qualified fuel design. [shard_04764_4126] [shard_04912_28668]

A utility should ask whether its proposed agreement is a fixed-price, indexed-price, or market-linked arrangement, whether it contains volume and delivery guarantees, and whether the supplier can demonstrate contracted access to conversion, enrichment, fabrication, transport, and backup inventory rather than only to uranium in the ground. [shard_01868_5915] [shard_04764_4126]

The agreement should also specify force-majeure treatment, sanctions and geopolitical substitution rights, notice periods, supplier-default remedies, replacement-fuel costs, minimum inventory, and who pays if a supplier must move material through a more expensive route. [shard_01427_71709] [shard_05762_6555]

The board should require diversification by supplier, country, route, and fuel-cycle stage rather than accepting a superficially diversified list of mines that all depend on the same Russian conversion or enrichment pathway. [shard_04912_28668] [shard_05762_6555]

It should also require the project company to report annually on forward coverage, on-site and off-site inventory, qualified alternative fabricators, non-Russian enrichment access, and the time required to qualify a substitute fuel. [shard_03095_68102] [shard_01427_71709]

An ordinary light-water SMR generally has the familiar low-enriched-uranium problem, with conventional fuel enriched to roughly 3% to 5% U-235, so its supply challenge is mainly access to diversified LEU, conversion, enrichment, and fabrication. [shard_04764_4126] [shard_02768_44044]

Many advanced reactors create a different and more serious early-stage risk because they require HALEU, defined as uranium enriched above 5% and below 20% U-235, and the commercial infrastructure to produce, transport, and fabricate it is not yet broadly established. [shard_05037_47072]

The HALEU market has been especially exposed because Russia and China have had the principal large-scale infrastructure, while Russian TENEX was described as the only commercial supplier at the time of the cited assessment. [shard_05037_47072] [shard_02508_35653]

HALEU also requires dedicated transport containers, specific fuel-cycle infrastructure, regulatory arrangements, and substantial capital investment, so a vendor promise that an advanced reactor “will use HALEU” is not equivalent to demonstrating a bankable fuel supply. [shard_05037_47072]

For any later SMR option, the board should make commercial commitment conditional on a demonstrated HALEU qualification and supply plan, named non-Russian suppliers, realistic production milestones, and a fallback design or fuel strategy if the promised HALEU schedule slips. [shard_05037_47072] [shard_02508_35653]

The practical decision rule is that conventional nuclear fuel risk is usually a manageable procurement and contracting issue rather than a gas-style exposure to immediate fuel-cost shocks, provided the project has diversified, multi-stage coverage and inventory. [shard_04516_9176] [shard_03095_68102]

It becomes a potential deal-breaker when the proposal relies on a single Russian-linked mid-cycle supplier, assumes Kazakhstan-origin material can always transit Russia, leaves fuel-price escalation uncapped, or makes plant operation depend on an unbuilt HALEU chain. [shard_04912_28668] [shard_05762_6555] [shard_05037_47072]

The board should therefore approve a long-term nuclear PPA only with explicit fuel-supply covenants and transparent pass-through limits, while treating an advanced-reactor or HALEU commitment as a separate infrastructure-development risk rather than assuming that the PPA solves it. [shard_01868_5915] [shard_05037_47072]
